lesson.title: The Zero That Isn't Zero: Understanding the Virtual Short
lesson.summary: A virtual short is the condition, present only when an ideal op-amp is operating with negative feedback in its linear region, in which the two input terminals sit at essentially the same voltage even though no wire connects them and no current flows between them.
lesson.body:
Start from the defining relationship of an op-amp, Vout = A_OL times (V+ minus V-), and rearrange it to solve for the differential input voltage: V+ minus V- = Vout / A_OL. This single rearrangement contains the entire idea behind the virtual short.

In the ideal op-amp model, A_OL approaches infinity. If Vout stays at some ordinary, finite value (a few volts, say, not clipped against the supply rails), then dividing that finite Vout by an infinitely large A_OL forces the quotient to approach zero. In other words, V+ minus V- approaches zero: the two input terminals converge to the same voltage.

This convergence only happens under two conditions, both worth stating explicitly. First, the op-amp must be wrapped in negative feedback, since feedback is what keeps Vout pinned to a finite, sensible value rather than slamming against a supply rail (an op-amp running open-loop, as the earlier open-loop gain chapter showed, produces wildly saturated outputs from the tiniest input imbalance). Second, the amplifier must be operating in its linear region, not saturated, since a saturated output is no longer described by Vout = A_OL times (V+ minus V-) at all.

Because V+ and V- sit at (nearly) the same voltage without being physically wired together, and because the ideal op-amp's infinite input impedance means no current actually flows between them to force that equality, the condition is called a virtual short. It behaves like a short circuit for the purposes of voltage, both terminals read the same voltage, but it is not a real short circuit, since a real short would allow current to flow freely between the two points, while here the current between V+ and V- is exactly zero by the infinite input impedance assumption.

It is worth revisiting just how small the residual gap really is. The ideal op-amp chapter worked out that a real op-amp with A_OL = 200,000 producing a 5 volt output requires a differential input of only 25 microvolts. Treating that 25 microvolts as exactly zero, which is what the virtual short assumption does, introduces an error far below the precision of ordinary circuit measurements and resistor tolerances.

The virtual short is the single most useful analytical shortcut in op-amp circuit design: instead of tracking the amplifier's internal gain at all, a designer can simply write V+ = V- and analyze the surrounding resistor network as if that equality were exact. The next chapter looks at a particularly common and useful special case, where one of those two terminals is tied directly to real, physical ground.
